The framing of software being "cared for" is a bit over the top, but it probably captures that what most people need is agency.  In terms of software, it is ownership of and responsibility for that software.   For making that software "insanely great".

comments.author: mpweiher
comments.text:
Fair question!

I still stand by that article.  Code that doesn't (need to) exist is preferable to code that was generated.

For a lot of glue code, I think I have an answer with Objective-Smalltalk.

But there is a lot of tedious code out there that I don't have an answer for.  Yet. :-) And not all of it is necessarily glue code.  And you also need to bring the existing sprawl into the brave new world of polymorphic architectural abstraction.

One example:  as one application of Objective-Smalltalk, I've been working on an "across-native" UI framework I call InterScript.  The idea is to have as rich a model as possible to then hook up to UIs that are as thin as possible, either native AppKit, UIKit, Android or HTMX/HTMXNative.  And have a (customizable) default UI generated for you a la naked objects or WebObjects Direct2Web.

So to get a table-view with some data, just create the table and "write" it to the UI generator (bound to the guy variable).

table ← #MPWDictArrayTable[
  #{ first: "Marcel", last: "Weiher" },
  #{ first: "Peter", last: "Alexander"},
  #{ first: "Hello", last: "World"},
  #{ first: "Hi", last: "There"}
].

gui ! table.


Now that's nice and concise, but it takes a good amount of code to get there.  Most of that code is not particularly exciting, and the idea of writing this code for AppKit, UIKit, Android and HTMX was...daunting to the point of not really being feasible for me, at least not with other things I also need to do.  Claude and to a lesser extent Codex helped me quite a bit here, and without that assistance I might never have embarked on the journey.   I give it UI to generate, then adapt it to the structure I need, though it's been getting better at figuring that out.

Similar with code-generation.  One example was that I early on had to make a choice as to whether to transpile to Objective-C or generate native code directly.  There are good reasons for both approaches. I decided to go with direct native, with good results.  Recently, I have decided to follow the Objective-C transpilation fork as well, because the effort required to do so is low enough that I can let that run on-the-side.  And also pursue an Objective-J transpiler to see if I can use Cappuccino to get some AppKit-like UI components for the Web (browsers, table-views).

Another example:  I am far from an expert on object-files and linkers, but the way of generating data in object-files seemed extremely manual, tedious and brittle to me.  I thought that at least for objects, I should be able to create a Mach-O serializer:  just write the object to the serializer and it places an appropriate binary representation in the Mach-O, with the data filled where needed and relocation entries/symbol entries for the pointers.

A lot of moving parts and my understanding of the subject matter is limited.  I had an AI generate the first version.  Despite me saying what I wanted, that version actually hard-coded generation for the initial data structures I had given as examples. It was also structurally wrong in a couple of places.  But it reduced the cognitive load enough for me to refactor that to what I wanted under the auspices of the tests.

So that's how AI generation has been liberating:  it allows me to tackle problems that would otherwise be too big, too daunting, or maybe seem too daunting. It gives me a first cut of something that I can refine and condense.  It allows me to have fewer context-switches between creating and critiquing.

So far there hasn't really been duplicated boiler-plate code that shouldn't exist.

Coding tools have gotten more powerful.  We can use that power to make it easier for us to produce slop, or we can set our sights higher, realizing that things that used to be firmly out of our reach might no longer be.

Per aspera ad astra.

comments.author: aatango
comments.text:
I think IKEA being the equivalent of bad quality is rather unfortunate, and, in my opinion, wrong.

From my experience, you get what you pay when buying at IKEA: the cheapest stuff might deserve the derision for low quality; I have found some really good quality-for-price furniture with them; and I feel they have very well made, if overpriced items too.

I still think comparing craft-made items against IKEA products makes sense, and rather with different angle: a crafts-person might make me a one-off, bespoke item that fits my specific needs and desires, whereas IKEA will happily sell me stuff from their pre-existing catalog, some of which might even be customizable.

If we take the metaphor towards software, I think the comparison is closer to a bespoke software that is built specifically for me, or me searching amongst the available vendors for the product that better fits your needs. Each offers a different experience. For example, a bespoke contract might include more on-hands support and feature requests are handled with priority. This might contrast with a off-the-shelf solution, which might have to prioritise amongst many stakeholders, and might not be as responsive to my requests. We could also discuss focus on quality, economy of scale, reinventing the wheel, competition between different actors, etc.


Hopefully there are still some people valueing good software, but for the vast majority of our society, IKEA it is.


If I understand your metaphor, "good software" implies craftsmanship, which implies increased cost, when comparing to an off-the-shelf solution.

I think this would be better phrased as: "hopefully there are still people willing to pay for good software". Everyone values good software, when it's the only criteria left to judge, for example, when all software costs the same. This unfortunately only seems to be the case with open-source projects that cost nothing and have a commercially friendly license, for which I have heard a fair amount of "war stories" of how stressful, and ungrateful it can be to maintain them.

Software can be "good" when it fits my needs, and its cheap to incorporate and use, regardless of how well crafted it is implemented.

comments.author: ombredog

I am really enjoying being a student after being in project/product management - so when I hear about developers turning into 'product management' like he mentioned about the guy using the agent, I kind of felt it maybe too hard.

For me, I think often there is some angle that treats everyday development too theoretical and not like the trade/vocation it is, but for learning?

With a chatbot, I am getting compressed weights from a transformer model with fun caching spewing tokens out so quickly without theoretical knowledge.

And these weights often are appearing too compatible with how my hippocampus wants to also compress that information further. So I passively make the executive decision that this is a solved problem, and I try to move onto the next thing... but I can't.

Someone could argue that is 'me holding back velocity', but whatever. I need to learn this stuff to think of novel concepts to then think of novel ideas. It could be in the model now, or not.

Even if it was 100% correct on my algorithm units, I don't think it would stay in my mind since I am not performing the vocational work of understanding why my brain needs to digest this.

It's a shame since I think we all broadly agree on maxims on when we pull out the calculator or not in our everyday jobs and in computing, I think we're using the calculator for everything around AI without understanding the application for it.

comments.author: tomsmeding
comments.text:
Perhaps the ubiquity of LLMs is indeed not the right target of blame here, true: in a different world, with different incentives around software engineering, and indeed economics and society at large, LLMs might have been taken up and used differently. Might have; I honestly kind of doubt that. It is true that the overblown state of the big AI companies fits well with how our (Western) economy works, but they would have been invented and developed regardless. Possibly more slowly.

However, our economy does not spring from a void; humans are susceptible to power. Not everyone is, but enough are, and enough are willing to follow someone with power, that these kind of structures have a strong tendency to form. And the point of the OP seems to be majorly that "AI chat was making [them] delusional." We have plenty of reports of this happening to people, even though it happens to far from everyone. And again, it's human nature: LLMs write in a way that exploits our internal heuristics for believability of information, which depend fairly significantly on how well the information is presented. (Others have already written about this.) Of course we can't be certain if LLMs would have had the same effect on society had they been introduced more slowly, and in a society less consumed by monetary greed, but I think we'd start seeing similar effects -- just more slowly.

All that is to say: if we can't blame AI for this, can we really blame society? Should we instead blame ourselves, perhaps, or how our brains work? That's hardly productive, unless you consider it productive to conclude that the human race had better not exist. (Which is, by the way, a point of view I find very difficult to refute.) So in absence of a good root cause to usefully blame, I think it's not so bad to blame AI, or at least the companies driving AI: if we can't fix the root cause, we'd better work around the worst outcroppings of our natures, and instead of doing that we seem to be diving headlong into the deep.

I think it's defensible to have a crisis about that.

comments.text:
I don't think that's what the other person was suggesting though.  Like they said, they'd rather have "smaller teams that consist of people who actually want to learn how to be better".

But at least in my experience, there are a lot of teams that have a mix of those people who are interested in getting better — and like you say, they are far more valuable than an LLM — alongside people who do not learn, and often don't want to learn, where you end up repeating the same things over and over again until they find a job somewhere else.  I've definitely worked with people where the work they were doing could have been solved so much more quickly if I'd given it to an LLM instead, and where that person learned absolutely nothing from the experience of doing it the slower way as well.

Or in other words, historically junior developers have done two roles in one: on the one hand, some to train up as a long-term alternative to hiring experienced developers; and on the other hand, cheap labour to write code or fix bugs because however good your experienced developers are, they have a limited bandwidth.  That second role is in part being replaced by LLMs, or at least it seems that way when talking to acquaintances actually working in various companies.  But the first role is still important and won't go away.  And while some companies will definitely get the wrong end of the stick and give up on juniors altogether, I am very sure that the market will eventually course correct and the value of junior developers will become clear again.

That said, this obviously isn't much help to junior developers looking for jobs right now, I imagine it's a pretty shit time.

comments.author: lukasl

If you want valid output, you need to the same you would do with a junior dev, be specific, pair with them, watch their work in small increments, never let them submit a large chunk of work. comments.author: lukasl
comments.text:
There are two arguments, why not teach a junior instead of using LLM, and why not write the code myself.

I prefer to only write the most challenging code myself and let LLm do then rest, plus running the builds and figuring out why the hell is the API I'm using not doing what I expected. That gives me energy to focus on what's more important, be it my personal life or another work. The best ideas come to me while doing gardening or doing other mundane tasks like that. If i was at the computer coding, the ideas would not come.

Why not teach a junior dev? I'd prefer to teach junior devs, who want to learn. I've been out of the hiring process for the last 5-6 years, but before covid, if we opened a position, we would get hundreds of CVs, interview the best out of them, and then realize none of them are good. Not in that they don't have the knowledge required, but there is lack of opportunity for growth. The process is seriously expensive and hiring the wrong guy to the team can be net negative for the entire team. I honestly sincerely believe it's for the best if there is some natural selection and people will have to come to the first job as seniors. That's will automatically filter out the people who actually care about the craft.

I think software architecture has often drifted into religion, because we don't actually have a way to make it concrete.  Code has pretty concrete feedback, and we've become pretty good at turning this into feedback loops, for example with agile techniques such as XP.

My thesis is that we need to make architecture concrete, which is why I've created the architecture-oriented programming language Objective-Smalltalk.

See:  Beyond Procedure Calls as Component Glue: Connectors Deserve Metaclass Status/
